rules.text: `odrl:isA` matching follows **only** the local `broader` chain, never `dpv_mapping`. A `broadMatch` to a generic DPV term would let an unrelated use satisfy a specific consent
Consent to a child purpose does **not** cover its parent
No governance file reaches an EDC without passing the gate
CI runs the gate on every change
The policy-id collision sweep detects collisions between policy ids and contract ids
`access_level: secret` means the dataset is never mapped or published
A `pii` dataset may never be transferred onward, derived from, distributed or sublicensed
Retention is expressed as a machine-readable duty on every dataset that declares one

rules.status_raw: Not enforced, and deliberately not emitted
rules.text: A policy's validity window (`valid_from` / `valid_until`) is enforced
CR-1, CR-2, CR-3 are implemented by the mapper's emission order and the consent registry's row precedence
CR-4 holds at every evaluation point
CR-5 holds during a running transfer, not only at negotiation
Every participant runs the policy enforcement capability; there is no unenforced participation tier (`AUP-08`)
An operand emitted by the mapper has a function registered for it in every scope it is bound to, and no operand is bound without a producer
Every participant implements or uses a catalogue service as part of its control plane (`DSSC-PUB-05`)
The federated index is advisory. A discrepancy between index and provider is resolved in favour of the provider
The index crawls only active participants
The index authenticates to the connector it crawls through
Access and usage control of offerings are expressed as ODRL policies (`DSSC-PUB-38`)
`dcat:keyword` carries no policy meaning. A dataset's permitted purposes come from `policy.purpose[]` and nowhere else
A catalogue includes at least one `dcat:DataService` referencing the service that provides its datasets (`DSSC-PUB-41`)
A catalogue response references its entries via `dcat:record` rather than inlining them (`DSSC-PUB-45`)
An offering missing any mandatory field is not published
A `pii` dataset with an unresolvable sharing offer is not published — advertising a consent gate that can never open is worse than not publishing
An empty `purpose[]` is never a wildcard for personal data
Metadata is checked for compliance with the standards it claims (`DSO-11`)
Metadata is checked for compliance with this rulebook (`DSO-12`)
Metadata is checked for completeness (`DSO-13`)
A publisher must be a registered participant, authenticated as such (`PUB-13`)
A publisher must be authorised for the *owner* whose datasets it publishes (`PUB-14`)
An unauthenticated or unauthorised publish, update or remove is **denied** (`PUB-19`, `-23`, `-26`)
A removed offering is no longer discoverable (`PUB-25`)
A discovering consumer must be a registered participant (`PUB-27`)
An unauthorised consumer's request must not even collect matching offerings (`PUB-32`)
Offering visibility may be restricted to a subset of participants (`PUB-03`)
Pseudonymised data is personal data. A dataset keyed by device id or subject DID rather than by name is still `pii`
Provenance records carry **codes, pseudonymous DIDs and hashes only — never PII**
A dataset may not be reclassified downward (from `pii`) without a documented assessment
Only `dpv:Consent` offers get a UI control

A **covered processor** — same controller, same operation, acting under a data processing agreement (GDPR Art. 28) — is disclosed, never asked. `POST /consent/request` returns 409 and `/internal/consent/check` returns `should_ask: false`, so the pending guard does not park a negotiation on a question that has no answer
A legal basis other than consent or contract requires legal analysis and appropriate protection measures before it is added to the vocabulary (`DSSC-XCT-07`, `-08`)

An empty `purpose[]` is **never** a wildcard for personal data. The person was never told the use, so consent would fail GDPR Art. 4(11). Fail closed — and this applies to the *requested* purpose too, not only the declared one
Purpose matching follows the local `broader` chain only, never the DPV mapping
Consent to a child purpose does not cover its parent
A purpose not in the active profile is a 422 at consent-write time, not a silently ignored value
The consent key is (subject, purpose, controller-role). Matching on controller alone is insufficient
An offer's `controller_role` must be one the file declares in `controller_roles`, and an offer naming a controller that *is* unbundled must say which function

A consent record carries a `legal_basis` evidence record: the DPV basis IRI, the consent-text version, the locale, a SHA-256 of the rendered text, the `user_visible_hash` and a submission reference. **Codes and hashes only, never PII**

The rendered-text hash is what proves *what the person was shown*. A translation may never widen a coverage window, change a resolution or invent a legal basis — the codes are authoritative and the frontend translates them
The wildcard admits any party **inside the circle** for that controller and purpose. It never admits a new controller and never a new purpose
A per-party row overrides the wildcard. An explicit grant and an explicit **opt-out** both win
The identity recorded against a consent ask is the DCP-verified counterparty, never a self-asserted header

Revocation terminates a **running** transfer, not merely future ones — **when it removes the last consent for that consumer and dataset**. While anyone else still consents, the transfer continues and the row filter drops the withdrawing subject's rows
A pending question that nobody can answer must not park a negotiation forever. A covered processor, and a purpose the offer does not carry, both resolve without asking
A subject may see every consent they hold and every ask outstanding against them
Subject-facing surfaces authenticate the subject's credential, never a service's scope. A service token must not be able to read one person's consents

Membership in an owner organisation is checked against the registry at consent-write time, not read from a JWT claim. The portal reads claims for UX; **data access decisions always go through the registry API**
A path-bearing subject DID must resolve, and its document asserts **no verification method** — the person holds no key
A person's DID sits in the namespace of the organisation that holds their credentials — `did:web:<participant>:users:<id>` — and **that** organisation publishes it
**One human, one identifier**, however many organisations hold credentials about them
Every participant records all **fifteen** types. Recording is not optional and not per-dataset (`PTO-40`, `-41`)
A consumer's *self-report* that it met an obligation is not provenance, and this platform records none
A `DataDisclosed` event carries a `consent_snapshot_hash` — a recomputable SHA-256 over the authorising consent tuples — proving *which* consent state backed the handover
Provenance records carry codes, pseudonymous DIDs and hashes only, never PII
An event is recorded once. Re-posting the same event is a no-op, not a duplicate
Every principal named in an event becomes an agent in the graph
The model is PROV-O. A participant storing logs in another model does not satisfy this rulebook

rules.status_raw: Enforced, by a sweep rather than by review.
rules.text: The JSON-LD `@context` defines every relation the ingest path can produce
A node's PROV-O type is a property of the node, not of the position it first appeared in
All principles from the Data Models building block apply to this data too (`PTO-59`)
A participant's provenance store is not readable by another participant
A subject may read the record concerning themselves, authenticated by credential rather than by service scope
Mandatory P&T data can be accessed and presented on demand (`PTO-79`)
A service reading lineage holds a scope that permits it
Recording must not slow the data path (`PTO-83`)
An event type has a schema, a materialiser and an emitter, or it does not exist
Provenance is retained for the life of the deployment and survives a participant's departure
Every offering declares its data format and content type
Every offering declares its refinement stage
Every offering declares the vocabulary its *policy* is written in (`odrl:profile`)
Every offering declares the semantic model its *payload* conforms to
A deployment records its payload models in its rulebook
The platform ships no payload model and imposes none
An offering's declared model must be resolvable — a bare name is not a model reference
Vocabularies are published in a machine-readable form, resolvable and unauthenticated
`schemas/` publishes every shape that crosses a repository boundary, generated from the models and never hand-edited, with a no-diff test
`schemas/purpose-vocabulary.json` is regenerated whenever the ODRL profile changes — it carries the slug `enum` the *active profile* accepts, which no static schema can
A vocabulary hub supporting editing and browsing exists (`DMO-19`)
A vocabulary change states the consents it would widen, or states that it widens none
The local hierarchy is authoritative for enforcement; external alignments are documentation
Deployment-owned payload models have their own documented management process
An organisation is not a participant until it has been promoted. Promotion requires a verified application, a resolved owner, and an accepted agreement
Promotion issues an `OrganizationCredential` signed by the trust anchor
Every participant holds at minimum a data space membership credential (`DSSC-IAM-08`)
Onboarding is idempotent — re-running it must not duplicate a participant, an owner, a credential or an agreement acceptance

rules.status_raw: Declared, and now carried by the credential.
rules.text: Assurance levels for verification are the deployment's responsibility (`DSSC-IAM-14`, KYC/KYB). For an **organisation** the platform records *that* verification happened (`verified_by`, `evidence_ref`); for a **natural person** the credential additionally records *who attested and by what method* (`verifiedBy`, `verificationMethod`)

A DID document is served only by the instance that holds that DID's key. A **subject** DID has no key and its document carries no verification method — it resolves so that consent records and provenance can point at it, and asserts nothing it cannot back
A DID's private key never leaves the instance that generated it, and is encrypted at rest. **The trust anchor holds no private key but its own, and a natural person has none**

A presentation query is answered only to a **verifier** that proves control of its own DID *and* presents an access token this participant's STS granted it. The grant's scope bounds what the presentation may contain (`DSSC-IAM-13`, proof of control)
The verifier's signature is checked against the key in **its own DID document**, resolved over did:web — never against a key this registry happens to hold
The revocation list is served signed, by the trust anchor, GZIP-encoded as StatusList2021 requires

**The same rule applies to a credential's issuer.** A service verifying a user Verifiable Credential resolves the issuer's DID document and reads the key out of it — never a key it was handed or mounted — and refuses an issuer the dataspace trust list does not carry as **active**
Every issued credential is allocated a distinct StatusList index
A credential's status bit is set **only** on revocation, never at issuance
Signature verification is never skipped, in any environment
The list of participants, including inactive ones, is published to participants (`DSSC-TRF-05`)

The list of **accredited entities** — trust anchors and trust service providers, **including revoked ones** — is published machine-readably and unauthenticated (`DSSC-TRF-05`, `-07`, `-17`, `DSSC-BIZ-143`)
Every entry names its **scope of attestation** (`DSSC-TRF-19`), and a trust service provider names the anchor it derives authority from (`DSSC-TRF-21`)
Withdrawing accreditation **marks an entry revoked with a reason; it never deletes it**
The revocation list is public and unauthenticated
Trust services validate attestations submitted by participants against the criteria (`DSSC-TRF-38`)
Every instance's encryption key must be backed up outside the cluster; losing one makes that instance's DID keys unrecoverable
Revoking a participant's membership credential removes their ability to negotiate — the DCP presentation query stops satisfying the membership constraint
Revocation does not retroactively invalidate completed transfers. What was lawfully transferred stays transferred; the obligations attached to it (retention, deletion) survive
Revocation of a *consent* is different from revocation of a *credential* and terminates a running transfer
A departing participant's provenance records are retained; they are evidence about the data space, not the participant's property

A participant's identity is **proved, never issued**: the organisation generates its own keypair, publishes its own DID document, and presents a self-issued token signed by that key to enrol (`DSSC-IAM-13`, proof of control). The anchor mints no participant key and no STS secret

A credential is issued only to a DID whose control has been proved, and is **delivered to the holder's own credential store** — the issuer keeps the issuance record, the holder keeps what it can present
**Where to enrol is discoverable from the anchor's DID alone**: its DID document publishes an `IssuerService` entry, and that URL is routed and serves issuer metadata
Conformity is **re-checked**, not asserted once at onboarding, against a machine-readable projection of this page (`DSSC-TRF-02`, `-03`, `-04`)
A participant that no criterion covers is a **finding**, not a pass
**Suspension is a state, not a slower revocation**: a verifier can tell the two apart, and a suspension can be lifted on the credential the holder already has (`DSSC-TRF-04`)

**Revocation is terminal.** Nothing transitions out of it, no path clears a revocation bit, and re-admitting a revoked organisation is a fresh verification and a fresh credential — not a reinstatement
Control-plane exchanges between participants use DSP `2025-1`. No other control protocol is accepted
A participant advertising a DSP endpoint without the `/2025-1` suffix is not reachable
The data plane is HTTP pull. Push, streaming and file-drop transfers are not supported
No data moves before the control plane has completed identification, authentication and authorisation (`DSSC-DEX-36`)
The data plane re-checks the decision on every request rather than trusting the EDR alone
The data plane must fail closed when the control plane is unreachable
**The negotiation gate must fail closed when the policy decision point is unreachable**
The data-plane endpoint handed to a consumer is the participant's own, not the provider's EDC
A query result is bounded. A provider may cap `limit` and must not be obliged to return an unbounded set
The query surface is dataset-scoped: a query naming a dataset the agreement does not cover is refused
A timeout is reported as a timeout, never as a terminal protocol state
A failed termination is reported as failed
The inventory above is authoritative and is updated in the same commit as any version change
The protocol publishes a machine-readable description of its capabilities and endpoints (`DSSC-DEX-38`)
The DSP version is changed only by the governance authority, never per participant
A version change is announced before it ships

open_non_conformances.detail: A policy's validity window is declared, reported by the `declared-not-enforced` check, and **not emitted** — because emitting a term nothing enforces is what this very row forbids. **Decided 2026-08-09: it stays declared.** Closing it means binding a date operand in `services/edc-extensions` first, and until something asks for date-bounded policies that is a Java change bought for a term no deployment uses. This is a stated incapacity, not a silent one
Metadata versioning is not implemented: a consumer cannot ask what an offering said when they negotiated. Blocked on a design decision — version the offering, or snapshot it into the agreement

Observability. Listed in §2 so it is not mistaken for a declared exclusion, and here because it is a rule the code does not keep. Steps 1 and 2 are done — reachability is gated per deployment, all four service charts emit a `ServiceMonitor` under the same flag, and the metric set is a table in the rulebook. **No tracing**: `OpenTelemetry` spans correlated by `dsp_agreement_id` are not started, and three of the four SLIs need them

No OpenAPI document for EDC's Management API. **Decided 2026-08-09: none will be published.** It needs a module outside the BOMs, and the surface is private to the deployment — a document describing an admin API nobody outside the deployment may call is documentation of an attack surface, not of an interface. The APIs a counterparty uses are DSP and DCP, and both are specified elsewhere
